title: Studies of Traditional Trees and Rocks

image.credit: Photograph via Wikimedia Commons (Dong Qichang - Studies of Traditional Trees and Rocks - 2005.9.3 - Minneapolis Institute of Art.jpg)

source.label: Sirén (citing the Wusheng shi shi): Dong retired to his home province, “where he lived for eighteen years”
Waley: Dong “completely identifies the Learned Man's Painting with the Southern School”

work.text: It has been said that in tree-painting one is free to make one's own style. Nothing could be more untrue! For willow-trees Chao [Po-chü] is the standard; for pines Ma Ho-chih; for withered trees Li Ch'eng.

source.author: Dong Qichang (Tung Ch‘i-ch‘ang)
source.title: Writings on painting
source.publisher: translated in Arthur Waley, An Introduction to the Study of Chinese Painting (Ernest Benn, 1923; Internet Archive scan)

work.text: It is most important that a landscape should include some withered trees. They should appear occasionally in among healthy trees, as a foil

source.author: Dong Qichang (Tung Ch‘i-ch‘ang)
source.title: Writings on painting
source.publisher: translated in Arthur Waley, An Introduction to the Study of Chinese Painting (Ernest Benn, 1923; Internet Archive scan)

moment.text: In other words, painters should combine real scholarship with extensive studies of nature, and in spite of their attachment to a certain tradition and their close studies of old masters, these scholarly painters were by no means indifferent to [observations of nature].
moment.lead: Sirén on Dong and his friend Mo Shilong:

source.author: Osvald Sirén
source.title: Chinese Painting: Leading Masters and Principles, vol. V (The Later Ming and Leading Ch‘ing Masters)

moment.text: Owing their position to assiduous study, they believed that knowledge was also the key to art.
moment.lead: Waley on the scholar-officials who practised “the Learned Man’s Painting”:

source.author: Arthur Waley
source.title: An Introduction to the Study of Chinese Painting

matters.text: I am over fifty; any trees, rocks, peaks or hillocks that I come across I can sketch quite successfully; but I still cannot do human figures, boats, carriages, or architecture; and this vexes me. I am glad, however, to recall that Ni Tsan suffered from the same defect.

source.author: Dong Qichang (Tung Ch‘i-ch‘ang)
source.title: Writings on painting
source.publisher: translated in Arthur Waley, An Introduction to the Study of Chinese Painting (Ernest Benn, 1923; Internet Archive scan)
